rv.q: Elyot provides a snapshot of men at a crunch-point.
Under Adam Spreadbury-Maher's direction, the acting and dialogue are naturalistic, the sexual scenes and descriptions frank — even full-frontal.

This play may be a tad dated, but I found it involving throughout, even if the denouement is rather obvious and its two hour length just right.
London is lucky to have a third opportunity to see this fascinating and emotional play which has been staged beautifully.

Both are in their 30s and live in a grubby flat in Kentish Town. The couple’s relationship is put under strain when Tony enlists the help of actor-cum-cleaner Robert – played wonderfully by fresh Rada graduate Jonah Rzeskiewicz – to sort out the flat.
Coming Clean is nevertheless a triumph in delivering Elyot’s quick wit and emotional depth.

cn.t: Elyot's 1982 debut captures a poignant pre-AIDS moment in gay London with wit and maturity, though critics split on the production's subtlety. Most praise the engrossing script's relevance, but some find the direction heavy-handed.
